newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Workers battle police in Seoul, crackdown imminent.
newsitem.headline: Workers battle police in Seoul, crackdown imminent.

text.p: Workers wielding iron bars and hurling rocks battled South Korean riot police on Wednesday and authorities warned strikes were being fanned by North Korea in a sign that a harsh crackdown on labour strife was imminent.
On the second day of what was billed as the biggest strike in South Korea's history, state prosecutors issued an ultimatum to union leaders to abandon stoppages or face arrest.

They stepped up pressure on seven leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions camped out in Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral by throwing a security cordon of riot police around the red-brick building.
Cabinet ministers added to a sense of crisis by saying strikes could undermine the economy.

In a sign Seoul was brushing aside world criticism of its tough stance, an international labour leader said the government had threatened to deport him and three colleagues if they had any more contact with union leaders.

Police fired volleys of tear gas to prevent some 15,000 workers and students from marching on Myongdong in some of the fiercest street clashes since a controversial labour law was rammed through parliament three weeks ago.
However, the final day of a planned general strike fizzled. Buses and subways ran smoothly and ports operated normally.

In the southeast city of Ulsan, Hyundai workers smashed picket lines to keep South Korea's largest dockyard open. They ran a gauntlet of unionists at the iron dockyard gates who lashed out at the strike-breakers with fists and threw buckets of yellow paint over their blue overalls.
It was the most dramatic indication that the hearts of rank-and-file union members were not in the fight against the new law that allows companies to fire workers and replace strikers.
State prosecutors invoked a North Korean threat, a move frequently used by past governments to justify harsh measures against political opponents.
"North Korea is agitating workers to topple the government," prosecutor Choi Byung-kook told a news conference.
"If the unrest drags on it will give North Korea an opportunity for revolutionary struggle."
The two Koreas have been enemies since their 1950-53 war ended in an armed truce.

The officially approved Federation of Korean Trade Unions said 400,000 of its 1.2 million members had walked out. The outlawed confederation, which says it has the support of 500,000 workers, said 350,000 of its members were striking.
The Labour Ministry said 111,000 workers joined stoppages.

A meeting of government ministers presided over by Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung determined that the arrest of unionists "cannot be delayed even with some negative effects and repercussions", a government statement said.
Political analysts said they thought a violent end to the strikes was inevitable since labour unrest had turned into an election-year battle against President Kim Young-sam.

Union leaders are calling for the repeal of the labour law railroaded through parliament on December 26 that breaks a tradition of jobs for life. They have organised wildcat strikes in the past three weeks that have hit key export industries.
The seven confederation heads are evading arrest by taking sanctuary on church grounds.

The head of the International Metalworkers' Federation, Marcello Malentacchi, said an immigration official had given him a letter outlining laws he and three other foreign labour leaders would violate if they met union bosses.
He said the immigration official told them: "Any participation or contact with Korean union leaders would be considered in violation of the law and result in deportation."
Malentacchi said he and the other three, in Seoul to show international worker solidarity, had already been due to leave South Korea at midday on Thursday prior to the threat.
But he added they would go ahead and meet confederation leaders several hours before their departure.
The South Korean currency, the won, was hammered by speculative selling, plunging to a six-year low over fears that prolonged unrest could threaten already slowing export growth.

Trade Minister Ahn Kwang-koo warned that stoppages could make it harder to control a snowballing trade deficit that hit $20 billion last year. Officials predicted economic growth would slow to six percent this year from 6.9 percent last year.
